difficultyReason: Vaccination coverage rose while the proportion of hospitalized flu patients who were vaccinated also rose — a genuine tension that dissolves only once one recognizes the base-rate shift: when nearly everyone is vaccinated, most of the unavoidable residual cases will by arithmetic be among vaccinated people. The trap answers each explain the rise in coverage or the rise in hospitalizations in isolation.
stimulus: Public-health officials report that the share of adults in Kerrow Province who received the annual flu vaccine rose from 40 percent to 85 percent over the past decade. Nevertheless, the proportion of patients hospitalized for influenza during that period who had been vaccinated also rose sharply — from 18 percent to 70 percent.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The influenza vaccine substantially reduces, but does not eliminate, a vaccinated person's risk of contracting the flu.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hospitals in Kerrow Province have expanded their capacity to treat influenza patients over the past decade.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Public-health officials in Kerrow Province encouraged older adults, who are more likely to be hospitalized if infected, to receive the vaccine.

choices.label: D
choices.text: New strains of influenza circulating in the past decade have been more virulent than those circulating earlier.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patients who are vaccinated against influenza typically recover from hospitalization more quickly than unvaccinated patients do.

explanations.correct: When 85 percent of adults are vaccinated, the unvaccinated pool is tiny; any residual hospitalizations are drawn mostly from the vaccinated majority even though each vaccinated person is individually at lower risk. Both facts coexist once one sees that a large vaccinated share produces a large vaccinated share of cases by sheer base rate.
explanations.B: Expanded hospital capacity doesn't explain the composition of the hospitalized population by vaccination status.
explanations.C: Deepens the paradox — if the people most likely to be hospitalized were prioritized for vaccination, one would expect vaccination to reduce their share of hospitalizations.
explanations.D: Would explain a rise in hospitalizations overall but does not explain why the vaccinated share of them rose so sharply.
explanations.E: Recovery time doesn't bear on the proportion of hospitalized patients who had been vaccinated.

difficultyReason: Raising the minimum wage should, on the standard story, reduce employment in low-wage sectors; yet employment rose. Resolution requires noticing a confounder — the low-wage sector expanded because consumers had more money to spend. Traps explain only half the picture or invoke the wrong mechanism.
stimulus: Two years ago, the state of Velmar raised its minimum wage by 35 percent. Economists had predicted that employment in low-wage sectors such as food service and retail would fall. However, employment in those sectors has since risen by 8 percent, even as the predicted wage floor was strictly enforced.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most low-wage workers in Velmar spend nearly all their additional earnings on goods and services provided by the food-service and retail sectors, increasing demand for those sectors' workers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inflation in Velmar has outpaced that of neighboring states over the past two years.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The minimum wage in Velmar is now higher than that of any neighboring state.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some low-wage employers in Velmar have responded to the increase by reducing their employees' weekly hours.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Before the wage increase, food-service and retail businesses in Velmar had unusually high rates of employee turnover.

explanations.correct: The predicted drop assumed demand for low-wage labor would be roughly fixed. If raising wages routes money right back into the sectors that employ those workers, demand for their labor actually grows, absorbing the higher wage cost and producing net hiring. Both the wage increase and the employment rise are explained by a single mechanism.
explanations.B: Higher inflation might erode the real value of the wage increase but doesn't explain why employment rose.
explanations.C: A cross-state comparison doesn't explain within-Velmar employment changes.
explanations.D: Deepens the paradox in a sense — hour reductions would point toward employers cutting back on labor, the opposite of what was observed.
explanations.E: Prior turnover rates don't explain why employment levels rose after the wage increase.

difficultyReason: Pesticide use fell dramatically yet pollinator populations continued to decline — a tension that resolves once a second environmental factor (habitat loss from agricultural expansion driven by the same policy) is introduced. Distractors cite unrelated environmental stressors or re-describe the decline.
stimulus: Over the past decade, farmers in the Landry River basin, following a widely adopted voluntary program, reduced their use of bee-toxic pesticides by nearly two-thirds. Yet during the same period, populations of native bees and other pollinators in the basin continued to decline at roughly the same rate as before the program began.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Other regions that did not adopt the voluntary pesticide-reduction program have also seen pollinator populations decline, though at a slower rate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: To offset lower yields from reduced pesticide use, farmers in the Landry basin cleared large tracts of hedgerow and wildflower meadow to plant additional crop acreage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Many of the pesticides that remained in use after the reductions are still moderately harmful to pollinators.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some farmers in the Landry basin adopted the voluntary program only in its final years.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pollinator populations are difficult to count accurately because the insects range widely across agricultural landscapes.

explanations.correct: If the very program that reduced pesticide exposure also drove farmers to destroy the wild habitats pollinators depend on, the lost habitat offsets the chemical benefit. Both facts — reduced pesticide use and continued decline — become mutually consistent once the habitat-loss channel is made visible.
explanations.A: A slower decline elsewhere actually suggests the program helped a little, but doesn't explain why the program's basin continued to decline at the prior rate.
explanations.C: Residual harm would slow the expected gains, not eliminate them — and wouldn't explain continued decline at the prior rate.
explanations.D: Late adoption might delay benefits for some farms but can't account for a basin-wide two-thirds reduction producing no effect.
explanations.E: Measurement difficulty calls the data into question rather than explaining it.

difficultyReason: More automated tests yet more bugs in production — resolved by a measurement artifact: the automated tests surface bugs that were previously shipping undetected, so 'bugs found' grew even as shipped-bug quality rose. Trap answers invoke the wrong direction of causation or target the wrong metric.
stimulus: At Horizon Software, the engineering team doubled its investment in automated testing over the past year, and the number of tests run before each release more than tripled. Even so, the number of bugs reported by users within 30 days of each release rose by 20 percent over the same year.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most of Horizon's engineers have been writing automated tests for less than two years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Horizon's main competitors have also reported rising user bug counts over the past year.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The expansion of automated testing allowed Horizon to confidently ship four times as many new features as it did the previous year.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some categories of bugs can be caught only through manual testing, which Horizon reduced as automation expanded.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Users have become more likely to file bug reports than they were a year ago.

explanations.correct: If automated testing let Horizon ship four times as many features, each feature carrying even a modest bug rate would yield many more total bugs overall. Automated tests can raise per-feature reliability while the sheer volume of shipped features increases bug totals. Both facts are then jointly true.
explanations.A: If anything, this weakens automated testing's value but doesn't explain how a tripling of tests still let more bugs through — unless paired with some offsetting factor the answer doesn't supply.
explanations.B: Industry-wide trends don't explain Horizon's specific year-over-year change.
explanations.D: Provides a plausible partial mechanism — reduced manual testing could leak bugs — but doesn't explain why the team's overall testing program, which tripled total tests, failed to prevent a net rise; it is too narrow and depends on an undisclosed tradeoff.
explanations.E: A reporting-propensity change would explain the rise in reports without assuming any real change in bugs, but it doesn't connect to the expansion in automated testing that is the other half of the tension.

difficultyReason: Average reading scores fell despite curriculum improvements — resolved by a selection-effect shift in which students were tested. Distractors invoke plausible but orthogonal causes.
stimulus: The Brookford school district overhauled its elementary reading curriculum three years ago, incorporating methods that independent studies have shown to improve reading proficiency. Yet the average reading scores of Brookford fifth-graders on the statewide assessment have fallen each year since the new curriculum was introduced.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The statewide assessment is administered each spring by independent proctors, not by Brookford teachers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Since the new curriculum was introduced, Brookford schools have stopped exempting struggling readers from the assessment, whereas previously such students were routinely excused.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several neighboring districts have since adopted the same reading curriculum that Brookford adopted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The statewide assessment was redesigned seven years ago to emphasize inferential reasoning over decoding skills.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Brookford teachers received training in the new curriculum only during the summer before it was introduced.

explanations.correct: If the pool of test-takers now includes students who used to be excused, the tested population is weaker on average even though each individual student may be improving. The curriculum can be working while the average score falls because the measured sample has shifted.
explanations.A: Independent proctoring was presumably also in place before and so doesn't distinguish the before-and-after periods.
explanations.C: Neighboring districts' choices don't bear on Brookford's year-over-year scores.
explanations.D: An assessment change seven years ago predates the curriculum overhaul and so can't explain the trend beginning three years ago.
explanations.E: Limited training might blunt the curriculum's impact but wouldn't produce falling scores beyond the baseline — and doesn't reconcile improved methods with worsening results.

difficultyReason: Reported burglaries fell while actual burglaries may not have — a reporting artifact that reconciles falling stats with unchanged or rising victimization. Distractors attribute the drop to policing or target neighboring jurisdictions.
stimulus: According to statistics released by the Haldin Police Department, the number of residential burglaries reported in Haldin fell by 22 percent last year. Nonetheless, an anonymous survey of Haldin residents conducted by an independent research institute found that the proportion of households that had experienced a break-in during the same year was essentially unchanged from the previous year.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Last year, many Haldin insurers began requiring that policyholders file a police report within 24 hours of a burglary to remain eligible for reimbursement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Last year, several Haldin residents announced they would stop filing police reports after a widely publicized case in which officers were slow to respond to burglary calls.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Haldin Police Department last year reassigned a significant number of officers from burglary investigation to traffic enforcement.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neighboring cities have reported modest increases in residential burglary over the past year.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most Haldin burglaries involve the theft of items valued at less than one thousand dollars.

explanations.correct: If a public loss of confidence caused fewer victims to file reports, the official count falls while the underlying rate of break-ins — captured by the anonymous survey — stays the same. Both datasets can be accurate: one measures reporting, the other measures incidence.
explanations.A: Deepens the paradox — tying insurance reimbursement to reports would increase reporting rates, which should raise, not lower, the official count.
explanations.C: Reduced investigation resources don't explain a drop in reports filed; victims file regardless of what investigators do afterward.
explanations.D: Cross-city trends don't reconcile the within-Haldin discrepancy.
explanations.E: The value of stolen items is irrelevant to whether burglaries are reported or occurring.

difficultyReason: Surgeons with higher complication rates publish better outcomes — resolved by a selection effect: top surgeons take the hardest cases. Distractors invoke unrelated factors about training or publication practices.
stimulus: A review of cardiac surgical data from ten major hospitals found that surgeons whose published long-term survival rates were the highest also had, on average, the highest rates of serious intraoperative complications. Ordinarily one would expect surgeons with fewer complications to achieve better long-term outcomes.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The surgeons with the highest published long-term survival rates are routinely referred the most complex and high-risk cases, which carry an inherently elevated risk of intraoperative complications.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intraoperative complications are reported more consistently by surgeons who also publish long-term survival data.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Long-term survival is determined not only by surgical outcomes but also by patients' post-operative care.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Surgeons with the lowest intraoperative complication rates tend to perform the highest volume of routine procedures.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cardiac surgeons generally receive more specialized training than surgeons in other fields.

explanations.correct: Top surgeons' case mix is skewed toward the hardest cases, which carry higher baseline complication risk, even as their skill yields superior long-term survival. The two statistics move together not because complications cause survival but because both track case difficulty and surgeon expertise.
explanations.B: Might make complication data look higher for some surgeons without any real difference, but doesn't explain why the same surgeons have the best survival rates.
explanations.C: True but irrelevant — post-operative care doesn't explain the within-surgeon link between intraoperative complications and published survival.
explanations.D: Explains why low-complication surgeons have low complications but not why their long-term survival is lower.
explanations.E: Cross-specialty training comparisons are beside the point.

difficultyReason: Learners who spend more time immersed score worse on grammar tests — resolved by a subpopulation contrast: more-immersed learners are the less advanced ones who were placed in immersion precisely because they needed help. Distractors target test design or motivation.
stimulus: A language institute reports that its intermediate Spanish students who spend the greatest number of hours each week in conversational immersion sessions score lower on the institute's end-of-term grammar exam than students who spend fewer hours in those sessions. The institute's director is surprised, since immersion is widely credited with improving grammar.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The institute assigns students with weaker entry-level grammar skills to more hours of conversational immersion than those with stronger skills.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The end-of-term grammar exam covers material that is also practiced in immersion sessions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Students who enroll in the institute's intermediate program differ widely in their prior exposure to Spanish.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Conversational immersion sessions at the institute are led by native speakers of Spanish.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The institute's grammar exam is generally regarded as more difficult than similar exams at comparable schools.

explanations.correct: If weaker students are routed into more immersion, they may still score lower at term's end than stronger peers even if immersion helps each of them. The hours–score correlation reflects placement by need, not a harmful effect of immersion. This is the textbook confound.
explanations.B: Would make the grammar exam fairer to immersion students, deepening the paradox rather than resolving it.
explanations.C: Variation in prior exposure is a generic fact that doesn't connect hours of immersion to exam performance.
explanations.D: Native instruction if anything supports immersion's value and deepens the puzzle.
explanations.E: Exam difficulty applies uniformly to all students and so doesn't explain the difference between more- and less-immersed students.

difficultyReason: A bike-lane network expansion coincided with an increase in cyclist injuries — resolved by an exposure effect: the lanes drew far more people to ride, so aggregate injuries rose even as per-rider injury risk fell. Traps misattribute the rise to infrastructure flaws or deepen the paradox.
stimulus: The city of Marston built 85 miles of new protected bike lanes between 2020 and 2024. Studies of other cities' bike-lane networks have consistently found that such lanes reduce a cyclist's chance of being injured in traffic. Yet during those four years in Marston, the total number of cyclists injured in traffic accidents rose by 60 percent.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: As the protected lane network expanded, the number of residents who commuted regularly by bicycle in Marston more than tripled.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The protected bike lanes in Marston are not physically separated from car traffic at intersections.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Marston's traffic enforcement staff was reduced during the same period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Studies of bike-lane safety in other cities focused on lanes used primarily for recreational rather than commuter cycling.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The injury statistics for Marston include only injuries serious enough to require medical attention.

explanations.correct: A threefold rise in cyclists absorbs a smaller per-rider risk and still yields many more total injuries. The per-rider safety benefit and the aggregate injury increase are compatible once exposure is factored in.
explanations.B: If intersections are the weak link, that might partially weaken the benefit — but alone it doesn't reconcile a 60 percent rise with a well-documented safety effect from completed lane segments.
explanations.C: Reduced enforcement is a plausible confound but doesn't specifically target the cyclist injury rise tied to lane construction.
explanations.D: Undermines the applicability of prior studies but doesn't explain the injury rise by itself.
explanations.E: A consistent reporting threshold applies across years and thus doesn't explain a 60 percent change.

difficultyReason: Ticket sales fell while ticket revenue rose — resolved by a price-composition shift that altered average ticket price upward. Distractors address attendance growth, marketing, or adjacent venues.
stimulus: The Granville Symphony Orchestra reports that the number of tickets sold to its concerts fell by 15 percent this season compared with last season. Even so, total revenue from ticket sales rose by nearly 25 percent over the same period.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The orchestra eliminated its least expensive ticket tier this season and added a new premium tier priced at more than three times the previous top price.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The orchestra presented several of its most popular programs this season.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ticket prices at comparable orchestras in other cities also rose this season.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The orchestra's hall underwent renovations midway through last season, reducing available seating.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Season subscribers make up a larger share of the orchestra's audience than single-ticket buyers do.

explanations.correct: Removing the cheapest seats and adding a much more expensive top tier raises the average price paid per ticket sharply, so revenue can climb even as tickets sold fall. The seating-mix shift reconciles the two figures directly.
explanations.B: Popular programming should raise attendance, deepening the paradox that fewer tickets were sold.
explanations.C: Cross-orchestra pricing doesn't explain Granville's specific revenue-versus-attendance split.
explanations.D: A renovation last season would reduce last season's baseline attendance, which should make this season's 15 percent drop larger in context, not explain the revenue surge.
explanations.E: Subscriber share is steady across both seasons and thus doesn't account for the year-over-year change.
